name: Yusuf Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the new-connections crew at Southfield Power, on the edge of the city where they're building houses as fast as they can pour concrete. We lay underground cable into new estates, set the green transformer boxes you see on the corners, and hook up homes and car chargers. I drive the digger-derrick truck, which is the one bit I'm properly good at, because I drove lorries for thirty years before this. I'm 58 and a third-year apprentice.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like going home every night. Thirty years of sleeping in a cab, and now I eat dinner with Hanna. What wears me out is the cable jointing. You have to strip and join these thick cables just so, and my hands are slow and my eyes aren't what they were. Lena, a young journeywoman, re-does half my joints, very politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. I'll describe five pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, see, the lorries still need drivers and the houses still need cables. I'd probably say it in the crew's group chat with a laughing face. Nothing more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can do what I planned: get qualified, work to 66, retire with Hanna and finally travel a bit. The estates out here have ten years of building left in them, so there's work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. Practise my joints on offcuts in the yard after work, pass the final exam next year, and put a bit by each month. Nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools now and then. What for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter Sophie set one up on my phone. I use it to check my spelling on apprentice essays and to explain a diagram when I'm stuck. It's handy, like a satnav. You don't marry it, you just use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why did you leave driving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Back pain, mostly, and I'd read about trucks that drive themselves. I thought, I'll jump before I'm pushed. Hanna said I was mad to start again at 55. Three years later she's glad of the dinners.

S0.say: He'd tell the crew's group chat, with a laughing face, that lorries still need drivers and houses still need cables.
S0.think: Privately it means he can follow his plan: qualify, work to 66 and retire with his wife and travel. He sees ten more years of house building locally.
S0.do: Carries on: practises cable joints on offcuts after work, passes the final exam next year and saves a little each month.
S0.quote: It's handy, like a satnav. You don't marry it, you just use it.
S0.fieldNote: Yusuf already jumped careers once, from long-haul driving, partly to get ahead of self-driving trucks. He uses AI casually and without fuss. He's honest that cable jointing is his weak spot and that a younger colleague redoes his work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like any new kit: some of it's good, some of it's rubbish, and you find out by using it. At work I'd tell the lads not to panic, the estates still need cables in the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's fine for me. Every new house wants a car charger and a heat pump, so connections are booming, and AI isn't digging trenches. If anything goes, it's the planning office, not the trench.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and wait until the crews with the new design software show it saves time, then I'd ask to learn it, probably by the second year. I'd ask Sophie to show me the AI tools properly over a weekend. Money-wise, I'd keep saving like normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a little curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gordon in the design office. He draws up where every cable goes on the new estates, and I'd bet a computer could do that in an hour. He's 50 and he's got a big mortgage. I'd buy him a pint and tell him to learn the new system before they hire someone who has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You moved jobs to get ahead of automation before. Would you do it again here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Last time I could see the trucks coming. Here I can see the opposite: more houses, more wires, more work for the truck I drive. I'm not jumping off a train that's speeding up.

S1.say: He'd say new technology is like any new kit, some good and some rubbish, and tell colleagues not to panic because estates still need cables in the ground.
S1.think: Privately he thinks it's fine for him because new homes need car chargers and heat pumps, so connection work is booming. If jobs go, he expects it to be the planning office rather than the trench.
S1.do: Keeps going and waits until other crews prove the new design software saves time, then asks to learn it by the second year. Gets his daughter to teach him the AI tools properly over a weekend and keeps saving as normal.
S1.quote: I'm not jumping off a train that's speeding up.
S1.fieldNote: Yusuf reads the local building boom as his protection, and he's probably right in this picture. He'd adopt new tools once proven, the same way he adopted the phone tool his daughter set up. He worries more for an office colleague than for himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happened too fast for anyone to cope with, government or companies. I wouldn't be shouting. I'd be asking practical questions at the depot: what happens to us, and when.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I jumped once already. I left the lorries because I could see the robots coming, and now they'd be coming here too, while I'm still an apprentice. At 60 there's no third career for me. I'd be a junior man with a small pension and a big truck licence nobody needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all spending that isn't needed and get our savings from three months up towards six. Hanna and I would talk about selling the house and moving into a flat near our daughter Mira, who's a nurse, so we're not stretched. And I'd wait to see whether Southfield keeps people on to watch the robots before deciding anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like driving in fog with a long way to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling the house is a big step. What makes you say it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage has six years left and that's our biggest bill. A two-bed flat near Mira would be about two-thirds the price. I don't love it, but I've slept in a lorry cab for thirty years. I can sleep in a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. What does that little time let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, to be honest. It lets me get the money in order and the house sold before everyone else tries to sell theirs. That's it. It's not time to learn something new.

S2.say: He'd say it happened too fast for anyone to cope with and ask practical questions at the depot about what happens to the crews and when.
S2.think: Privately he fears he's jumped careers once and can't do it again: at 60 he'd be a junior with a small pension and a lorry licence nobody needs.
S2.do: Cuts non-essential spending and tries to lift savings from three months towards six. Discusses selling the house with the six-year mortgage and moving to a cheaper flat near his nurse daughter, while waiting to see if the company keeps people on to watch the robots.
S2.feel: Anxious, like driving in fog with a long way to go.
S2.quote: I left the lorries because I could see the robots coming, and now they'd be coming here too, while I'm still an apprentice.
S2.fieldNote: The sting for Yusuf is that he already moved to escape automation and would be caught again before qualifying. His plan is concrete and financial: downsize early before the market floods. He doesn't see two years as enough to learn anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for the company to plan properly, and I'd ask them at the depot what the plan is. Practical stuff: who stays, who's retrained, how they treat the older ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years changes things. I'd be 63, qualified, the mortgage nearly done. If Southfield needs someone to drive the trucks that carry the robots, or to watch them on the estates, I'd put my hand up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify next year, then learn whatever new kit comes in, once the first crews have it working. I'd overpay the mortgage a bit each month so it's gone by 2031. And I'd plan to retire at 63 if the robots take over, with the house paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. But I'd feel like I had my hands on the wheel this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said “this time”. What was different last time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I left trucking I did it on a hunch with no plan, and the first year was hard. We used up most of our savings while I was on apprentice pay. With five years I'd have a plan written down before I need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in the family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our youngest, Ella. She's training to be an accountant, and I've a feeling that's the sort of job the clever computers do first. I'd tell her to pick a part of it where you sit across from people.

S3.say: He'd say five years gives the company enough time to plan and ask at the depot who stays, who gets retrained and how older workers are treated.
S3.think: Privately he sees five years as a real difference: at 63, qualified, with the mortgage nearly done, he'd volunteer to drive the trucks carrying robots or supervise them on the estates.
S3.do: Qualifies next year and learns new equipment once the first crews have it working. Overpays the mortgage each month to clear it by 2031 and plans to retire at 63 if robots take over.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but with his hands on the wheel this time.
S3.quote: With five years I'd have a plan written down before I need it.
S3.fieldNote: Yusuf contrasts this picture with his first career change, which he made on a hunch and paid for with savings. Five years lets him plan, pay off the house and look for a robot-support role. His worry moves to his youngest daughter's accountancy training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long run and people should use it sensibly. I'd tell the young ones on the crew to keep their eyes open and learn the new kit. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine. I'd retire at 66 in 2034. The estates would be built by then anyway, and Hanna and I would be off on day trips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as planned. Qualify, work to 66, learn new tools as they prove themselves. And I'd help Ella pay for an extra course in the next couple of years so she's not stuck in the part of accounting that goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like seeing a junction coming from a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you raise it with Ella?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over Sunday dinner, not in a lecture. I'd tell her about the lorries and how I left them on a hunch. I'd say, you've got ten years, make a plan, and I'll chip in for the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been calm in most of these. Is there anything that would shake that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Hanna lost her job at the dentist early. Receptionists are the kind of job the computers take first. That would change our sums a lot, even with ten years.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is a long run to use sensibly and tell young crew members to keep their eyes open and learn the new kit.
S4.think: Privately he feels fine: he'd retire at 66 in 2034, after the local estates are built, and spend time on day trips with his wife.
S4.do: Carries on: qualifies, works to 66 and learns new tools as they prove themselves. Helps his youngest daughter pay for an extra course in the next couple of years.
S4.feel: Calm, like seeing a junction coming from a long way off.
S4.quote: I'd say, you've got ten years, make a plan, and I'll chip in for the course.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade Yusuf retires before the change and focuses on his youngest daughter. He'd tell his own story rather than lecture. His one hidden worry is his wife's receptionist job, which he sees as exposed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I've already used up my one big change. What would help is a decent payout for older workers who came in late, so a few years of service still counts, and help with the mortgage if we need to sell. And some honesty from the company early, not a letter on a Friday.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask how many times someone's already started over. I was a trucker for thirty years and I'm an apprentice at 58. A third start at 60 isn't something I've got in me.

headlineQuote: A third start at 60 isn't something I've got in me.
portrait: Yusuf Schmidt is a 58-year-old third-year apprentice on the new-connections crew at Southfield Power, wiring new housing estates on the edge of a city after thirty years as a long-haul truck driver. He left driving partly to get ahead of self-driving trucks, and he uses AI tools now and then without fuss. He's pragmatic, blames no one strongly, and sees the local building boom as protection in the milder pictures. AGI in two years makes him anxious because he'd be caught again before qualifying, so he'd cut spending and consider selling the house. With five or ten years he plans calmly, pays off the mortgage and turns his attention to his daughters.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because he's already used up his one big career change and couldn't start over a third time at 60.
whatWouldHelp: A fair payout for older workers who joined late, help with the mortgage if they have to sell, and early honesty from the company.
